Volume 16 · Chapter 09

Robustness, uncertainty and external validity

Research Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v16-c08

By the endEvaluate whether a conclusion survives plausible alternative assumptions and populations.

Find the boundary of the conclusion

Capability. Evaluate whether a conclusion survives plausible alternative assumptions, analyses and populations. Bring the estimand and analysis plan from research design, power and preregistration. A robustness exercise is useful when it exposes what an argument depends on. It is not a contest to accumulate favorable regressions. The three cases below are original synthetic teaching artifacts about bank credit; they are not completed empirical studies or evidence for a real policy.

A conclusion has several parts: a population, intervention, outcome, horizon, effect size and uncertainty statement. “Credit rises” might mean a positive point estimate at treated banks, a confidence interval excluding zero for an eligible roster, or a beneficial nationwide effect after other lenders respond. Those are different claims. Before changing a specification, write which part stays fixed and which part changes. Otherwise a sequence of positive coefficients can hide movement between targets.

Robustness asks whether a stated conclusion persists across a defensible set of alternatives. Sensitivity analysis quantifies how that conclusion changes as an explicit assumption is relaxed. Sampling uncertainty comes from the observation or assignment process. Identification uncertainty remains when the available distribution and assumptions permit different effects. External validity concerns applicability beyond the study setting; transportability asks what assumptions and information justify a specified new population's effect. None is resolved merely by computing a small standard error.

1. Choose alternatives for reasons that precede their results

Start an audit with the primary estimand and the main threat. Ask whether the proposed alternative repairs that threat, probes an assumption, changes measurement or changes the question. Changing a pre-treatment precision adjustment can leave the outcome and population fixed. Dropping non-takers changes an assignment-effect target and conditions on behavior after assignment. Replacing net advances in millions with log gross lending changes the measured outcome. Excluding small banks changes population weights. These alternatives may deserve study, but their coefficients cannot be counted as repeated estimates of the original object without an explicit bridge.

A specification family needs an inclusion rule, not just a long menu. Record the economically defensible choices, prohibited combinations, sample and variable definitions, estimator assumptions, and what was known when the family was selected. Remove redundant reparameterizations: duplicating an equation under a different name adds no independent evidence. Preserve results from included choices that weaken the conclusion. If a newly discovered data error requires another analysis, document the discovery and amendment instead of pretending that choice was made earlier.

The primary Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson specification-curve paper motivates a defensible, nonredundant family, a display linking estimates to decisions, and joint inference that recognizes dependence. We use those bounded organizing ideas. Our tiny family, finite randomization test and bank data below are separately constructed and proved; we do not reproduce the paper's empirical applications or adopt a general resampling guarantee.

A descriptive specification curve orders estimates and shows the decisions that produced them. Sorting can reveal which adjustment matters. The range of estimates is not a confidence interval, and the share with a positive sign is not a probability that the effect is positive. All analyses reuse much of the same information. A joint inferential procedure must reproduce their dependence and the actual selection/assignment mechanism. An observational study does not acquire a valid permutation test merely because software can shuffle labels.

Worked case 1. A complete small specification curve with joint inference

Target and data. Eight fictional banks form a fixed eligible roster. Exactly four are chosen uniformly for an early offer. The target T is the equal-bank average effect of the offer on current ninety-day net borrower advances Y, in millions. X is net advances in the preceding ninety-day period, measured before assignment in the same units. The offer cannot change X; no interference is assumed. The displayed assignment offers A–D. These are invented observed data, not a full potential-outcome schedule.

Complete original analysis data; Z is offer assignment
BankZPrior flow XCurrent flow Y
A1812
B11015
C11216
D11421
E068
F088
G01012
H01212

Declared family. Compare unadjusted current-flow means; compare changes Y−X to impose a persistence coefficient of one; and fit a common-slope regression Y=α+δZ+βX+error. The first is transparent about the randomized contrast. The second may improve precision when prior flow predicts current flow with coefficient near one. The third estimates that persistence instead of fixing it, at the cost of additional estimation and model dependence in a small sample. All retain the full roster, same assignment and current-flow target. We do not search over outlier exclusions, post-treatment controls or outcome transformations.

The first two estimators are design-unbiased for T: each bank's offer probability is one-half, so the expectation of the current-flow mean difference is the roster average effect; the expectation of the pre-treatment X mean difference is zero. Subtracting that baseline difference preserves the target. This argument does not make every realized estimate correct. The regression coefficient is an adjustment diagnostic; interpreting it as a model-based estimate of a common effect additionally requires a defensible common-slope, constant-effect conditional-mean model. We do not claim general finite-sample design-unbiasedness for the estimated adjustment. Its later use as a sharp-null test statistic needs no correct regression model.

Calculate every estimate. Offered and control X means are11 and9; Y means are16 and10. The unadjusted estimate is6. Changes have means5 and1, giving4. For the regression, remove each arm's mean from X and Y. The within-arm sums Σ(X−X̄z)² are20 and20; cross-products Σ(X−X̄z)(Y−Ȳz) are28 and16. Thus β̂=44/40=11/10. The fitted intercept difference is δ̂=(16−10)−(11/10)(11−9)=19/5. In family order, estimates are (6,4,19/5) million. The normal equations justify the formula: minimizing over each arm's intercept centers its residuals, and differentiating the remaining sum of squared centered residuals gives β̂=SXY/SXX; SXX=40>0 ensures a unique slope and intercepts.

The estimates share a positive sign but differ materially in size: baseline adjustment accounts for the observed prior-flow imbalance. The range [19/5,6] describes this family's point estimates only. Eight banks do not become twenty-four observations by fitting three equations. To evaluate a null jointly we must specify a law, not vote among the three signs.

Exact joint test. Use the sharp null Yi(1)=Yi(0) for every bank. Under it, the observed Y vector remains fixed for all possible assignments. For each of the70 equally likely four-bank offer sets, refit all three specifications and calculate M=max{|δ̂current|,|δ̂change|,|δ̂adjusted|}. All are in millions. This unstudentized maximum is deliberately chosen in advance; it can favor a noisier statistic but is valid under the stated randomization law. The regression is well-defined for every assignment in these data: X has five distinct levels, whereas an intercept plus a binary Z could span X only if X had at most two levels.

The observed M is6. Exactly6 assignments produce M≥6, so the exact inclusive-tail p-value is (6,70,3/35) for (tail count,total count,p). It exceeds0.05. We therefore do not reject this sharp null at5%, even though all three estimates are positive. Nonrejection does not establish zero effects. This is one joint test, not three individual tests or a confidence interval for the average effect.

Why the test controls size. Under the sharp null and uniform assignment, each of the70 statistics is equally likely. For any observed value m, p(m) is the fraction of the list at least as large as m. Order the list from largest to smallest, keeping ties in their full upper-tail groups. At most a fraction α of assignments can belong to groups with upper-tail fraction at most α. Hence Pr(p≤α)≤α. Dependence among specifications is retained because each assignment refits the whole family. This proof needs the sharp null to impute outcomes; it does not establish a test of the weak null that the average effect alone is zero when individual effects differ.

The following complete standard-library program performs that enumeration. The dataset is embedded; all fractions are exact. It was executed during preparation. It neither estimates a real bank effect nor shuffles an observational treatment without an assignment argument.

from fractions import Fraction as F
from itertools import combinations

X = tuple(map(F, (8,10,12,14,6,8,10,12)))
Y = tuple(map(F, (12,15,16,21,8,8,12,12)))

def estimates(offered):
    t = tuple(offered)
    if len(t) != 4 or len(set(t)) != 4 or any(type(i) is not int or not 0 <= i < 8 for i in t):
        raise ValueError("four distinct bank indices required")
    c = tuple(i for i in range(8) if i not in t)
    mean = lambda v, group: sum(v[i] for i in group) / len(group)
    dx = mean(X,t) - mean(X,c)
    dy = mean(Y,t) - mean(Y,c)
    xx = sum((X[i]-mean(X,g))**2 for g in (t,c) for i in g)
    xy = sum((X[i]-mean(X,g))*(Y[i]-mean(Y,g)) for g in (t,c) for i in g)
    if xx == 0:
        raise ValueError("common slope is undefined")
    return dy, dy-dx, dy-xy/xx*dx

if __name__ == "__main__":
    observed = estimates((0,1,2,3))
    reference = [max(map(abs,estimates(t)))
                 for t in combinations(range(8),4)]
    cutoff = max(map(abs,observed))
    tail = sum(m >= cutoff for m in reference)
    print("estimates:", ",".join(map(str,observed)))
    print("tail,total,p:", tail, len(reference), F(tail,len(reference)))

The exact output is estimates: 6,4,19/5 followed by tail,total,p: 6 70 3/35. A completed reporting sentence is: “The three declared estimators range from3.8 to6 million and all are positive; the prespecified joint sharp-null test yields p=3/35. The family does not establish a nonzero average effect, validate the common-slope model or address unmeasured outcomes.” Changing the family after looking at its curve requires a new selection-aware argument or an exploratory label.

2. State how much assumption failure the conclusion can tolerate

Changing a control set is often an indirect probe of identification. A more interpretable analysis specifies the departure itself: how large could selection bias, counterfactual trend error or measurement bias be, in the outcome's units? A sensitivity parameter is not an estimate of that failure unless a separate design identifies it. Its plausible range needs substantive justification from the measurement process, prior evidence or a mechanism. A convenient range selected because the answer survives it is circular.

The retained scoped reading of Rambachan and Roth separates restrictions on counterfactual departures from sampling uncertainty. Here we use only that distinction; the following one-dimensional additive-bias benchmark is derived independently. It is not their parallel-trends procedure or a guarantee for arbitrary observational estimators.

Worked case 2. A bias budget and two different tipping points

Contract. In a different hypothetical observational analysis, θ is the population contrast estimated by θ̂, τ is the causal mean effect sought, and θ=τ+b. Bias b is fixed but unknown. Suppose θ̂ is normal with mean θ and known standard error s>0. This is a fully specified probability benchmark; estimated standard errors, clusters and nonnormal sampling would need their own justification. Values (1.2,0.4,0.6) give observed θ̂, s and a proposed upper bound B, all in millions. Assume 0≤b≤B: selection may inflate the contrast but cannot deflate it. That one-sided restriction is substantive, not implied by the estimate.

At a fixed b, θ̂−b estimates τ and the central95% interval is [θ̂−b−zs, θ̂−b+zs], with z=Φ−1(0.975)≈1.959964. Varying b in [0,B] gives an adjusted-estimate range [θ̂−B,θ̂] and the union confidence interval [θ̂−B−zs,θ̂+zs]. Do not call the adjusted-estimate range a confidence interval or an identified set based on a known population θ. θ is still estimated.

Coverage proof. Let E be the event |θ̂−θ|≤zs, whose probability is0.95 under the stated law. For every allowed true b, τ=θ−b lies between θ̂−b−zs and θ̂−b+zs on E. That individual interval is contained in the displayed union, so the union covers τ with probability at least0.95 uniformly over b∈[0,B]. The same central-error event supports all these bias adjustments; no independence across bias values is assumed. The interval may be conservative. This is repeated-sampling coverage for each allowed data-generating process, not a posterior95% probability for τ and not a claim that the bias range is correct.

Without bias adjustment, the95% interval is (0.416014,1.983986). At B=0.6, adjusted point estimates range from0.6 to1.2, yet the union interval is (-0.183986,1.983986). Thus all adjusted point estimates are positive while the sensitivity interval includes zero. A report that calls the conclusion robust because its adjusted estimate never changes sign would omit sampling uncertainty.

The point-estimate sign reaches zero at B=θ̂=1.2. The lower confidence endpoint reaches zero at B=θ̂−zs≈0.416014. Those two tipping values are (1.2,0.416014). Strict positivity of the union's lower endpoint requires B below the second value, not equal to it. For a proposed substantive threshold τ>0.5 million, even B=0 fails to put the lower endpoint above0.5. These are different decisions: positive estimate, confidence separation from zero, and confidence separation from an economically meaningful threshold.

Completed sensitivity decision. “Selection bias up to0.6 million is a scenario assumption requiring external defense. Within it, adjusted point estimates remain positive but the95% union interval admits zero and small negative effects. This study cannot support a uniformly positive-effect claim under that budget. We will report the full profile and seek information capable of narrowing the bias range.” If bias could have either sign, |b|≤0.6 instead yields (-0.183986,2.583986). The lower endpoint is unchanged, but the upper endpoint rises. More observations can narrow s; they do not by themselves reduce B.

3. Change populations explicitly, then question structural stability

Internal validity concerns the study's causal contrast; external validity asks about a specified destination. An effect modifier is a pre-treatment characteristic across which the intervention's average effect differs. If a target contains more low-response banks, its mean effect can differ even when every stratum's response is stable. Weighting can address a measured mix difference; it cannot establish that all relevant modifiers were measured or that policy implementation is unchanged.

The retained Dahabreh and coauthors'2019 author manuscript makes transport assumptions and overlap explicit. We use that bounded conceptual scope, not its uninspected general inference results. Define S=1 for a source population and S=0 for a target. Let H and L be high and low pre-offer external-funding dependence, measured consistently in both populations. Write τs(x)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)|X=x,S=1] and τt(x) analogously. The outcome remains ninety-day net advances in millions.

For the following standardization, assume source assignment identifies each τs(x), the intervention and outcome mean the same thing in both populations, and conditional mean effects are stable: τt(x)=τs(x) for every target stratum. Require overlap: positive target mass only where source effects can be learned. Target stratum proportions must also be known or estimated with uncertainty. Conditional equality of effects is sufficient for the mean-effect formula; equality of entire outcome distributions is stronger than needed. It is nevertheless a substantive assumption about unobserved target counterfactuals.

Tt=Σxpt(x)τs(x)=Es[w(X)τs(X)],   w(x)=pt(x)/ps(x).

Proof. By total expectation, the target average is Σpt(x)τt(x). Conditional effect stability substitutes the source effects. Under overlap, multiplying and dividing each summand by ps(x) gives the weighted source expectation. The weights satisfy Esw=Σpt=1. This algebra supplies no information for a target stratum absent from the source and no test of conditional stability. Extreme weights also concentrate finite-sample information; an exact population identity need not yield a precise estimator.

Worked case 3. A transport memo, a support failure and a scale-up counterexample

For this arithmetic exercise, treat source stratum effects and shares as known population inputs, not estimates from the eight-bank sample. In order(H,L), let source effects be (2,1/2) million, source shares (3/4,1/4), and target shares (1/4,3/4). The source average is(3/4)2+(1/4)(1/2)=13/8. The transported target average is(1/4)2+(3/4)(1/2)=7/8. These averages are (13/8,7/8). Copying the source average into the target overstates the model-implied target effect by 3/4 million.

The source weights are (1/3,3): high-dependence banks are downweighted and low-dependence banks upweighted. Their source-weighted average is1; the weighted source effect is7/8. These are population density ratios, not unnormalized counts or bank-size weights. If target H share is only known to lie in[1/10,2/5], the target effect is1/2+(3/2)pt(H), increasing in that share, so its range is (13/20,11/10). This is scenario uncertainty about composition, not a sampling confidence interval.

Overlap failure. Now consider a different target with shares(H,L,U)=(1/5,3/5,1/5), where U is a new type absent from the source. The known contribution is(1/5)2+(3/5)(1/2)=7/10. If a substantively defended scenario restricts τt(U) to[−1,3] million while H and L remain stable, the target mean lies in (1/2,13/10). The endpoints come from7/10+(1/5)(−1) and7/10+(1/5)3. These bounds are sharp under exactly the stated restrictions: assign every U bank effect−1 or3 for the endpoints, or any intermediate common effect to attain every interior mean. No observed source outcome is changed. Without any bound on U, its positive target mass makes the target mean unrestricted over the real line. Renormalizing the known80% to100% would instead estimate the target's supported subpopulation, a different object.

Structural-stability failure. Return to the original target shares(1/4,3/4). Suppose scaling up the offer changes competing lenders' behavior or funding prices, so target conditional effects are(1,−1/2) instead of(2,1/2). The actual target mean would be -1/8 million, despite the stable-response calculation7/8 and a positive source mean. This counterexample changes the response structure; it does not refute source randomization or the arithmetic of reweighting. If scale affects outcomes, write potential outcomes with the relevant policy environment, such as Y(z;g), and define whether g is held fixed or changed. A source individual-offer effect at one saturation is not automatically the effect of nationwide implementation at another.

The completed transport memo reads: “Our destination has fewer high-dependence banks. Conditional on a common offer, common measurement, overlap and stable conditional effects, standardization implies0.875 million rather than the source1.625. Those are population arithmetic inputs for this exercise; real estimated effects and shares require uncertainty propagation. We must audit missing modifiers and unsupported types and investigate scale-induced competition or funding responses. If the environment changes, the stable-response transport claim stops; a new design or model is required.” Matching observed covariate distributions is a useful diagnostic, not proof of the unobserved effect-stability restriction.

4. Write the uncertainty statement at the level of the claim

A complete audit states the primary result, why each alternative was included, whether the target changed, what survived and what did not. It gives the joint inferential procedure for a searched family or labels the display descriptive. It reports a sensitivity parameter in interpretable units, defends its range separately from the result, and distinguishes uncertainty in observations from uncertainty in assumptions. For a destination population it names the population weights, effect modifiers, support failures and implementation conditions.

Use a stop or narrowing rule with a concrete consequence. If outcome construction cannot be reconciled, stop the common-outcome comparison. If the source has no support for a meaningful target group, report a defended bound or narrow the target explicitly. If a plausible bias budget crosses the confidence tipping point, withdraw the uniformly positive claim. If scale changes equilibrium responses, do not call simple reweighting a policy forecast. More robustness columns cannot repair a missing identification bridge. A well-supported boundary is a research contribution even when it weakens the preferred headline.

Exercises

  1. Using the eight-bank data, compute the unadjusted and change-score estimates. Prove why both target the same roster average assignment effect in design expectation. Explain why deleting non-takers or replacing Y with log gross lending is a different exercise.
  2. Derive the common-slope adjustment from within-arm centering, compute the slope and offer coefficient, and identify the extra interpretation assumption. Explain why its point estimate is not another independent observation.
  3. Reproduce the joint sharp-null test, stating the assignment count, statistic, observed value, inclusive-tail count and p-value. Prove its size bound and explain why it is not a test of every zero-average-effect schedule.
  4. With θ̂=1.2,s=0.4 and0≤b≤0.6, compute adjusted-estimate range and95% union interval. Give the point and confidence tipping budgets, including whether equality supports strict positivity.
  5. Keep those inputs but allow |b|≤0.6. Derive the interval. Then halve s while returning to0≤b≤0.6; compute the new lower endpoint and explain which uncertainty improved.
  6. Compute source and target average effects from the two-stratum inputs. Derive the standardization formula and list the required causal/transport restrictions. What changes if the target high-dependence share is uncertain in[1/10,2/5]?
  7. Compute the two source density-ratio weights, their source average and the weighted source effect. Explain why dropping a sparsely represented target group or capping its weight changes the calculation unless the resulting bias is addressed.
  8. For target shares(1/5,3/5,1/5), derive and prove the sharp mean-effect bounds when U's effect lies in[−1,3]. What is learned without that bound? What is the supported-subpopulation mean after excluding U?
  9. With original target shares and conditional effects(1,−1/2), compute the target average and its gap from the stable-response prediction. Identify which assumption fails and explain how scale-dependent potential outcomes change the research question.
  10. Write a short audit memo for the claim “our positive credit result is robust and applies nationally.” Use all three worked artifacts, give one concrete next information need for each, and state an honest narrower conclusion. This is a critique of the claim, not a request to perform a real study.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. Same outcome, different adjustments

Y means16 and10 give6; X means11 and9 give2; subtracting yields4, also the difference between change means5 and1. Under the four-of-eight lottery, expected offered and control outcome means are the respective full-roster potential-outcome means; their difference is T. Since X precedes assignment, both expected baseline means equal the same roster X mean, so their difference has expectation zero. Subtracting it preserves unbiasedness. Removing non-takers selects on a post-assignment variable and changes who is averaged; log gross lending changes the outcome and its units. Neither is simply a different precision adjustment to the specified net-advance ITT effect.

2. Solve the adjusted comparison

For any fixed β, the best intercept in each arm is Ȳz−βX̄z. Substitution leaves centered residuals, so minimizing their squared sum gives β̂=Σ(X−X̄z)(Y−Ȳz)/Σ(X−X̄z)²=(28+16)/(20+20)=11/10. The offer coefficient is the intercept difference6−(11/10)2=19/5. A common-slope, constant-effect conditional-mean model supports interpreting that coefficient as the common effect; general exact design-unbiasedness is not established by the regression calculation. The same eight Y observations and assignment generated all three numbers, so their agreement is dependent evidence, not three independent studies.

3. Joint inference respects the assignment

There are8!/(4!4!)=70 equally likely offer sets. Refit all three estimators on each and take the largest absolute coefficient in millions. The observed maximum is6; six assignments reach or exceed it, giving6/70=3/35≈0.085714, so no rejection at0.05. The complete code supplies the exhaustive calculation. Under the sharp null outcomes are fixed and each reference-list entry is equally likely. Upper-tail ranks with ties included can place at most fraction α of entries at p≤α, proving size at most α. A zero roster average with offsetting individual effects does not fix the counterfactual outcomes under reassignment; the same reference list then need not be its null distribution. Three positive estimates neither prove a positive average nor invalidate the nonrejection.

4. Bias and sampling jointly

The adjusted-estimate range is[0.6,1.2]. With z≈1.959964, zs≈0.783986, the union interval is[1.2−0.6−0.783986,1.2+0.783986]=[−0.183986,1.983986]. Point positivity reaches zero at B=1.2, while the interval's lower endpoint reaches zero at B≈0.416014. Strict positivity requires B smaller than the relevant boundary; equality gives zero. The proof uses the single central sampling event for θ̂−θ and then allows every b in the fixed budget. It does not estimate b or give a probability that the budget is correct.

5. Direction and precision matter differently

When b∈[−0.6,0.6], take the smallest adjusted lower endpoint at b=0.6 and largest upper endpoint at b=−0.6. The interval is[−0.183986,2.583986]. Returning to b∈[0,0.6] but s=0.2 gives lower endpoint1.2−0.6−1.959964(0.2)=0.208007 and upper endpoint1.591993. This benchmark interval excludes zero under the maintained one-sided budget. Sampling precision improved, while the maximum permitted bias stayed0.6. Even taking s toward zero would leave an assumption-driven span of width0.6; precision alone cannot justify the bias restriction.

6. Standardize to the destination

The source mean is(3/4)2+(1/4)(1/2)=13/8; the target mean is(1/4)2+(3/4)(1/2)=7/8. Total expectation gives the target-weighted conditional target effects; conditional mean-effect stability replaces them with source effects. Source effects must be identified by the stated assignment/consistency/no-interference conditions, target support must be covered, X and the intervention/outcome must have common meanings, and target weights must be known or their uncertainty considered. If target H share is between1/10 and2/5, the affine increasing mean1/2+(3/2)p spans[13/20,11/10]. That composition scenario range is not a confidence interval for estimated inputs.

7. Weights do not create support

w(H)=(1/4)/(3/4)=1/3 and w(L)=(3/4)/(1/4)=3. Their source average is(3/4)(1/3)+(1/4)3=1. The weighted effect is(3/4)(1/3)2+(1/4)3(1/2)=7/8. Dropping a target group alters target composition. Capping weights changes the weighted distribution, so it no longer implements this identity; it may trade variance for bias and needs an explicit target or sensitivity analysis. A stable mean of weights near one is not evidence that conditional effects transport.

8. Bound the unsupported group honestly

The supported contribution is7/10. Adding(1/5)τ(U), with τ(U)∈[−1,3], gives[1/2,13/10]. To attain any value in the interval, assign U a common effect between−1 and3 while preserving all H,L effects and source observations; hence no tighter bound follows from these restrictions. With U unrestricted, any real target mean can be produced by choosing τ(U)=5(T−7/10). Excluding U and renormalizing gives(7/10)/(4/5)=7/8 for the supported80%, not the full target. Its numerical equality to the earlier two-stratum target mean follows from these chosen H:L proportions and does not restore missing support.

9. A stable mix is not a stable response

The target mean is(1/4)1+(3/4)(−1/2)=−1/8. Its actual-minus-predicted gap is−1/8−7/8=-1 million. Conditional mean-effect stability fails; overlap and the source experiment can remain valid. If outcome Y(z;g) depends on policy saturation g, moving from source g to target g changes the relevant causal contrast. Reweighting source individual-offer effects at fixed g is not the effect of changing g for the whole economy. The research needs information about those responses, not just a better estimate of target H share.

10. An audit memo that limits the headline

A complete response is: “The three declared estimates are positive, but their joint sharp-null p-value is3/35; the curve's range is descriptive and does not demonstrate a nonzero average effect. Audit the assignment and family declaration before expanding this test. In a separate observational benchmark, allowing upward bias0.6 leaves positive adjusted point estimates but a95% union interval including zero; obtain substantive evidence about measurement or selection sufficient to defend a narrower bias budget. For a target with a different dependence mix, stable conditional effects imply7/8 rather than13/8; collect comparable modifier distributions and information on missing types and scale responses. Our supportable conclusion is that specified calculations reveal favorable point estimates under some maintained conditions, with explicit inferential and transport limits. No national policy effect or uniformly positive causal claim has been established.” Grade against the three distinct threats, correct quantitative implications, one relevant new information need for each, and a narrower conclusion. These are separate teaching settings; combining their numbers into one empirical estimate would fail the exercise.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why three positive estimates, a small standard error and balanced observed population weights answer three different questions. Answer guide: the estimates share observations and need joint inference; a small standard error does not bound bias; weight balance does not establish overlap or conditional response stability. Give one failure case from each worked artifact.

After one week: reconstruct the two tipping budgets in case2 and explain why the unsupported U group prevents point identification in case3. Answer guide: the adjusted estimate crosses zero at θ̂ while the lower confidence endpoint crosses at θ̂−zs; positive target mass with an unrestricted missing stratum permits every real target mean. A defended bound or an explicitly narrower population changes the claim honestly. Carry the audit memo into writing a research paper, keeping every conclusion attached to its assumptions and evidence.

Sources and further study

  • Uri Simonsohn, Joseph P. Simmons and Leif D. Nelson — Specification curve analysis — Family validity/nonredundancy, decision-linked descriptive display and dependent joint inference, physical1–5.
  • A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends — Reduced-form/departure decomposition, relative-increment versus curvature sensitivity, and the difference between identified and confidence sets. Compact fibers and original square sharpness are proved directly, as is a separate finite known-Gaussian projection.
  • Dahabreh et al. — Extending inferences from a randomized trial to a new target population (arXiv v3, 2019) — Explicit nonparticipant target, participation/treatment assumptions, standardization and weighting; finite-cell proof to be original.
